intro.t: Where everything starts: creation, the fall, and God's promise to Abraham.
b: Genesis divides cleanly in two. Chapters 1–11 deal with the whole human race — creation, the fall, the flood, Babel — and answer why a good world contains so much that is wrong. Chapters 12–50 narrow to one family, beginning with God's promise to Abraham of a people, a land and a blessing that will reach every nation. Everything the rest of the Bible does is that promise working itself out.

Traditionally ascribed to Moses. Read it for the shape of the story rather than for isolated lessons: the first three chapters set up a problem that the last three chapters of Revelation resolve, and the correspondence is deliberate.

1.t: No argument for God's existence is offered anywhere in Scripture; it begins by assuming it. The verse also rules out matter being eternal and God being part of creation.

1.h: How Christians read the six days
1.t: What this chapter teaches is not in dispute among Christians: God created everything out of nothing, deliberately, in order, and called it good, with humanity made last and in his image. How long it took is disputed, and honestly so. Some read the days as ordinary days; some as long ages; some as a literary framework arranging the acts of creation rather than timing them. All three are held by people who take Scripture as God's word. We would not make any of them a test of fellowship, and we would be cautious of anyone who does. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

The plural has been read as majestic, as divine council, and as an early hint of plurality in God. Whichever, the image is given to humanity as male and female together, and it carries a commission: fill, subdue, rule — the first job description.
The repeated refrain becomes emphatic at the end. Whatever is wrong with the world now, the text is clear it was not made wrong.

2.t: Humanity is made of the ground and animated by God's own breath. Both halves matter, and the Bible never treats the body as the regrettable part.

We hold that he was, and that this is not a side issue. Paul's argument in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15 sets one man's disobedience against one man's obedience, and it is hard to see how the comparison works if only one of the two ever existed. Some evangelical scholars now read Adam as representative rather than as the first individual; we think that costs more than it saves. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.
The first thing declared not good in a very good creation is a man on his own. The word for the woman means a corresponding strength, not a subordinate — it is used elsewhere of God himself.

3.t: The serpent's method is to question, then to contradict, then to reframe God's motive as self-protective. The sin is presented as a bid for autonomy rather than an appetite for fruit.
Shame, hiding, and then blame passed along the chain. The consequences are relational before they are anything else.
The offspring of the woman will crush the serpent's head and be struck in the heel. Christian readers have seen the whole gospel in outline here since the earliest centuries.

4.t: Sin is described as crouching at the door, desiring him. The question 'am I my brother's keeper' is left unanswered by God and answered by the rest of Scripture.

6.t: The diagnosis is total and internal. God's grief in verse 6 is stated without embarrassment. Noah found favour — the first appearance of grace in the Bible.
Righteous and blameless among the people of his time — and the ark's dimensions are given precisely, as if to say this was a real object.

9.t: The reason given for the seriousness of murder is the image, which grounds human dignity in something other than capacity or usefulness.

11.t: A tower to make a name for themselves, and the scattering that follows. Acts 2 deliberately reverses it.
He leaves Ur for Canaan and settles halfway, at Haran. The call to Abram in chapter 12 finishes a journey his father abandoned.

12.t: Land, people, and blessing to all the families of the earth. Paul calls the last clause the gospel announced in advance. Everything from here to Revelation is this promise being worked out.
Three verses after the promise, he lies about his wife to save himself. Genesis never cleans up its heroes.

15.t: Abraham believed God and it was credited to him. Both Paul and James build on this verse; it is the seed of the doctrine of justification.
In the covenant ceremony both parties should pass between the pieces. Only God does. He takes the whole obligation on himself.

22.t: The hardest chapter in Genesis. Note the phrase 'God will provide for himself the lamb', the substitute caught in the thicket, and that the place is named 'the LORD will provide' — on a mountain in Moriah, where the temple would later stand.

22.h: Why would God ask Abraham to do this
22.t: This is one of the hardest chapters in Scripture and it is right to find it disturbing. Three things help. First, the reader is told at the outset it is a test, and God stops it; child sacrifice is condemned elsewhere in the law as detestable, so the chapter is not endorsing it. Second, Abraham tells his servants that he and the boy will both come back, and Hebrews 11:19 says he reasoned God could raise the dead. Third, the substitute is provided on the very mountain where the temple would stand, and 'God will provide the lamb' is fulfilled when the Father does not spare his own Son. The chapter points beyond itself. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

50.t: Joseph's summary of the whole narrative and one of the clearest statements in Scripture of how God's sovereignty and human responsibility operate together. Both intentions are real; only one prevails.

5.h: The genealogy that ends in death
5.t: Eight times the refrain: and he died. The exception is Enoch, who walked with God and was not. Genesis is establishing the reach of chapter 3.

7.t: Note that God shuts the door. The narrative is careful to say the waters covered the mountains and that everything with the breath of life died.

8.h: A new start, with the same problem
8.t: God's promise never to destroy the earth this way again is given because the human heart is evil from youth — the same reason given for the flood in 6:5. Mercy is not conditional on improvement.

16.t: The God who sees. She is the first person in Scripture to give God a name, and she is an Egyptian slave woman.

17.t: The covenant sign given to Abraham. Paul's argument in Romans 4 depends on the fact that he was already counted righteous before this chapter.

18.t: Down from fifty to ten. The audacity is remarkable and God does not rebuke it, which says something about what prayer is permitted to sound like.

19.t: Grim reading. Ezekiel 16:49 names the city's sin as arrogance and refusing to help the poor and needy, alongside the events here. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

21.t: Isaac means 'he laughs'. Sarah laughed in disbelief in chapter 18 and laughs in joy here; the name holds both.

25.t: Esau despised his birthright. Hebrews 12:16 uses him as the warning example of trading something permanent for something immediate.

28.t: Jacob is running away after deceiving his father, and God appears and makes promises to him anyway. Jesus applies this image to himself in John 1:51.

32.t: All night, and Jacob will not let go without a blessing. He leaves with a new name and a permanent limp, which is about right.

37.t: The coat, the dreams, the brothers' hatred. The narrative turns on human wickedness that God will later say he meant for good.

39.t: Joseph does the right thing and is imprisoned for it. The refrain four times is that the LORD was with him — including in prison.

45.t: The reconciliation. He weeps so loudly the Egyptians hear it, and tells them not to be distressed because God sent him ahead to preserve life.

13.t: Having been promised the land, he lets his nephew pick. Lot chooses by what looks well watered and ends up near Sodom.

14.t: A priest-king of Salem with no genealogy given. Psalm 110 and Hebrews 7 both build on that silence.

20.t: Abraham repeats the deception about Sarah. Genesis reports his relapses as flatly as his faith.

24.t: The longest chapter in Genesis, and almost all of it is a servant praying and then telling the story of his prayer being answered.

27.t: Rebekah engineers it, Jacob executes it, Isaac cannot undo it. Nobody in the chapter behaves well and God's promise runs through it anyway.

29.t: The man who impersonated his brother wakes up married to the wrong sister. The narrator does not comment; he does not need to.

33.t: Jacob expects four hundred men and gets an embrace. Twenty years of dread resolved in a sentence.

41.h: From the dungeon to second in Egypt
41.t: Joseph credits the interpretation to God before he gives it. The rise is sudden and the waiting was thirteen years.

42.t: They do not recognise him. Joseph's harshness here is usually read as testing whether they have changed.

49.t: Jacob's blessing on his fourth son, and the line the Messiah is expected to come through.

10.t: Seventy nations descended from Noah's sons. The list is theological as much as ethnographic: every people on earth comes from one family, which is the ground for the promise in 12:3 that all of them will be blessed.

23.t: Abraham, promised the whole land, owns exactly one field of it at his death — bought at full price to bury Sarah. Hebrews 11 says he died still waiting, and this chapter shows it.

26.t: The only chapter about Isaac as the main figure. He repeats his father's lie about his wife and reopens his father's wells. Faith is shown passing down a generation, flaws included.

30.t: Rachel and Leah compete through children and servants, and Jacob's flocks multiply through a breeding scheme. God works through a family behaving badly, without endorsing any of it.

31.t: Twenty years of sharp dealing on both sides end with a boundary heap and a treaty. Rachel's theft of the household gods shows how incomplete the family's faith still was.

34.t: A grim chapter of violation and brutal revenge. The text reports it without approval, and Jacob's deathbed words in chapter 49 condemn Simeon and Levi for it. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

35.t: Jacob orders the foreign gods buried before returning to where God first met him. Renewal begins with putting things away.

36.t: A full chapter for the brother outside the line of promise. Genesis does not forget him, and Edom's story runs on through the prophets.

38.t: An uncomfortable interruption in the Joseph story. Judah's line — the line of David and the Messiah — continues through Tamar, whom Matthew names in Jesus' genealogy. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

40.t: Joseph credits God before interpreting the dreams, then asks to be remembered. The cupbearer forgets for two full years.

43.t: Judah offers himself as surety for Benjamin — the first sign that the brother who sold Joseph has changed.

44.t: The longest speech in Genesis, offering himself as a slave in Benjamin's place. It is the moment Joseph can no longer hold back, and a picture of substitution.

46.h: Do not be afraid to go down
46.t: God speaks to Jacob at Beersheba and promises to go with him into Egypt and bring him back. The family moves under promise, not in exile.

47.t: He buys up the land and people for Pharaoh in exchange for food. Readers are divided on whether this is presented as wise administration or as the beginning of the slavery Exodus opens with.

48.t: Jacob blesses the younger grandson above the elder, deliberately. The pattern of God choosing the unexpected runs right through Genesis.
